transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-29
Time: 08:00 PDT / 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 mins
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Oliver Reed (Keystone CTO), Sana Malik (Head of MLOps), Derek Wu (SRE)
Shared artifacts: Redwood Optimize deck (https://redwood.ai/share/optimize-keystone), benchmark spreadsheet (link shared in chat)

Summary:
Redwood AE+SE walked Keystone Payments through Redwood Optimize recommendations focused on batching and prefix/KV caching to reduce per-token costs while meeting a P95 latency target of ~150-200ms for their payment fraud detection assistant. Discussed tradeoffs between hosted vs dedicated capacity, KV cache hit rates, and a simple cost model showing latency/cost curves. Agreed next steps for a 4-week pilot and to run a small benchmark with Keystone's sample prompts.

Topics:
- Current stack & constraints (real-time fraud NLU, 70 qps average, spikes to 300 qps)
- Latency SLOs and tail latency concerns
- Batching strategies and dynamic batching windows
- Prefix / KV cache configuration and warmup policies
- Cost model with token-level unit economics and expected savings
- Security (SOC2/KMS, private deployment options)

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, with Liam our SE. how's everyone doing?
[00:00:08] Oliver: Good, thanks, yeah excited to see the Optimize walkthrough, trying to get numbers we can take to the execs.
[00:00:15] Maya: Awesome, quick agenda, we'll run through the cost model, batching strategies, prefix/KV cache behavior, then leave time for nitty gritty networking and security.
[00:00:28] Liam: Hi all, I'll dig into the runtime specifics and show a couple of examples, please stop me if anything is unclear.
[00:00:37] Sana: Quick background, our use case is a fraud-prevention helper that augments rules with LLM signals, typical prompt length 120-250 tokens, we have about 70 qps steady, but legal and holiday spikes to 250-300 qps for short windows. SLO is P95 <= 200ms ideally.
[00:01:05] Liam: Got it, so prefix caching looks like a big lever here, since you have a high percentage of similar prompts, is that right?
[00:01:12] Sana: Yeah about 60% of requests share the same transaction-context prefix, the rest are more ad-hoc investigative prompts.
[00:01:20] Derek: quick note, our infra team needs to know if we do Private deployment we'll have to route through a NAT box, so egress may add some ms.
[00:01:29] Maya: Yep noted, we'll cover Private routing implications. so first, batching — there's a couple of knobs; static batch windows vs adaptive.
[00:01:42] Liam: Right, our runtime supports continuous batching with micro-batches every 8-20ms depending on load, and you can configure a max batch size. In practice for your qps we see better latency with short windows + concurrency instead of waiting long to fill large batches.
[00:01:58] Oliver: I guess I'm worried about cost, larger batches improve throughput but increase latency per request sometimes?
[00:02:05] Liam: It's a tradeoff, larger batches amortize model compute so cost per token drops but tail latency can increase if you wait to fill the batch. But with our dynamic batching it will auto-cut when latency threshold reached, so you rarely see long waits.
[00:02:21] [00:02:21] Sana: can you quantify? like if we choose max batch 32 vs 8 what do we expect?
[00:02:29] Liam: Sure, ballpark: at your token lengths, batch 8 gives P95 ~140-170ms with per-token cost X, batch 32 could drop cost by ~20-30% but P95 may increase to 220-300ms if you enforce long fill times. But with adaptive windowing you can capture most of the cost benefit without sacrificing P95; the cost model we shared in the sheet has curves.
[00:02:55] Maya: I'll point you to the sheet in chat, see the "Batching vs Latency" tab — we modeled token costs using our hosted GPU profile and a dedicated 8-GPU pool.
[00:03:08] Oliver: we run on a mix of short and long prompts, how does KV cache help here?
[00:03:14] Liam: Two cache modes: prefix cache (we cache KV cache of the prefix so subsequent completions don't re-compute prefix attention) and richer KV cache which persists KV across requests for the same session key. For your workload with 60% shared prefix, a prefix cache hit rate of 50-60% reduces token generation by roughly that percent on the model side.
[00:03:36] Derek: what's the warmup time, and does cache eviction add complexity? we have plenty of churn in session ids.
[00:03:42] Liam: Warmup is quick — first request pays the full cost, subsequent hits are fast, typically 30-50% latency reduction shown in our microbenchmarks. Eviction policy is LRU by default and you can configure TTLs. For high churn with many session ids, you'd tune TTL lower and consider combining prefix cache with rate-limited batching.
[00:04:01] Sana: any gotchas with KV cache and quantized models? we run int8 in some places.
[00:04:07] Liam: Good question, quantization sits below the cache — the KV cache stores activations, it's independent of weight quantization. Some smaller diff in latency due to memory ops but generally it plays nicely. we did note in one region we had a mismatch in a vendor name in logs it was transcribed weirdly but functionally it's fine.
[00:04:25] [00:04:25] Oliver: security wise, we need KMS integration and audit logs, can Redwood support HSM-backed keys?
[00:04:32] Maya: Yes, for Private we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) and we emit audit logs. We'll attach SOC2 and our security whitepaper in the follow-up.
[00:04:43] Derek: latency overhead for Private deployment? earlier you said egress could add ms.
[00:04:49] Liam: Typical added network roundtrip is 5-25ms depending on routing and NATs. If you colocate in the same region or use VPC peering it's minimal. For strict P95 targets we usually recommend Dedicated in-region or a Private with direct peering.
[00:05:05] Sana: what's the expected cost savings with caching + batching together? we need a conservative estimate.
[00:05:11] Liam: Combined you can expect 30-50% per-token compute savings in many payment use cases — crucially depends on cache hit rate and batch utilization. In the sheet we put a conservative scenario: 40% hit rate and moderate batching yields ~35% cost reduction versus non-batched hosted baseline.
[00:05:29] Maya: we also showed break-even for Dedicated at your qps — if you sustain above ~120 qps average, Dedicated capacity plus caching becomes cost-effective versus pure hosted.
[00:05:40] Oliver: can you run a quick walkthrough of the benchmark steps we should run?
[00:05:44] Liam: Sure, step 1: provide a representative prompt set (you mentioned 1k samples) and traffic profile. Step 2: we'll run a synthetic replay against a canary model with config variants: no cache, prefix cache only, prefix+session KV cache; batching windows small/medium/large. Step 3: collect P50/P95/P99 latency, throughput, and token counts to feed the cost model. Step 4: review together and pick pilot config.
[00:06:10] Sana: how intrusive is instrumentation? we don't want to ship new agents across prod just for testing.
[00:06:15] Liam: We can run benchmarks from our side with a replay harness or provide a lightweight script you run in staging. The benchmark harness can mimic qps patterns without changing prod.
[00:06:27] Derek: about evictions again, if we have sudden surges of new session ids during fraud waves will cache thrash and hurt latency?
[00:06:34] Liam: If you have a working set bigger than cache memory, yes hit rate will drop; mitigation: tune TTL to be shorter and rely more on batching during waves, or use a hot-key cache for the most common prefixes. Also, a hybrid where we push hot prefixes into a pinned cache segment for some minutes.
[00:06:52] Oliver: competitor question — why not just use our current self-hosted runtime and add batching there?
[00:06:58] Maya: You could, but Redwood's value prop is runtime optimizations + orchestration; we handle kernel selection, continuous batching, and automated fallback, plus the cost modeling and monitoring to show unit economics. It saves engineering time and risk.
[00:07:15] Sana: any sample dashboards we'll get for pilot?
[00:07:19] Liam: Yes, Redwood Console will show token-level cost, per-route latency, batch utilization, and cache hit metrics. We'll share a sample dashboard and the queries.
[00:07:30] [00:07:30] Maya: quick demo — switching to the sheet, here's the cost model, the x-axis qps, y-axis monthly cost, different curves for hosted/dedicated with/without cache.
[00:07:42] Maya: see this point at 80 qps hosted without caching is $X, with prefix cache at 50% hit it's $0.65X, dedicated with similar hit looks like $0.55X but you need committed spend.
[00:07:57] Oliver: commitment worries — what happens if traffic drops after we reserve Dedicated?
[00:08:03] Maya: We offer flexible commit tiers and burst options; our typical suggestion is start with a smaller commit for predictable baseline and use burst capacity for spikes, we can model scenarios in the spreadsheet.
[00:08:17] Sana: about regen / function calling flows we use — do caches interfere with tool calls?
[00:08:24] Liam: Tool calling outputs are considered part of the response; KV/prefix caching concerns only the model activations. If your tool calls mutate context you may invalidate caches; we recommend keying cache by stable prefix only and invalidating on explicit context changes.
[00:08:41] Derek: network test — we'll want to run a traceroute and synthetic latency tests before pilot.
[00:08:46] Maya: absolutely, we'll send a runbook for that.
[00:08:50] Oliver: can we do a 4-week pilot? ideal timeline: week 0 onboarding, week 1 baseline run, week 2 cache/batching variants, week 3 review & tune, week 4 wrap and exec summary.
[00:09:02] Maya: that timeline sounds good to us. We'll align internal SE and infra folks.
[00:09:09] [00:09:09] Sana: final question on telemetry retention and PIIs — we need retention policies and redaction.
[00:09:16] Maya: We support configurable retention windows and can redact specific fields; for Private deployments customers can keep logs on-prem or direct to their SIEM, we'll include details in the security pack.
[00:09:28] Oliver: ok great, I think we have enough to move forward, thanks.
[00:09:32] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the pricing + SOC2 + benchmark sheet.
[00:09:38] Liam: I'll kick off the benchmark repo and share scripts.
[00:09:42] Derek: I'll coordinate with our networking folks and send traceroute results.
[00:09:46] Maya: recap of next steps — send pricing, security docs, run benchmark, confirm pilot scope.
[00:09:54] Oliver: perfect, talk soon.

End of transcript.
